On the global well-posedness of the Boussinesq system with zero viscosity

Taoufik Hmidi & Sahbi Keraani
Abstract.

In this paper we prove the global well-posedness of the two-dimensional Boussinesq system with zero viscosity for rough initial data.

1. Introduction

This paper is a sequel to [12]. We continue to study the global existence for the two-dimensional Boussinesq system,

(Bν,κ)​{∂tv+v⋅∇v−ν​Δ​v+∇π=θ​e2,∂tθ+v⋅∇θ−κ​Δ​θ=0,div​v=0,v|t=0=v0,θ|t=0=θ0.({B_{\nu,\kappa}})\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}v+v\cdot\nabla v-\nu\Delta v+\nabla\pi=\theta e_{2},\\ \partial_{t}\theta+v\cdot\nabla\theta-\kappa\Delta\theta=0,\\ \textnormal{div}\hskip 1.9919ptv=0,\\ {v}_{|t=0}=v^{0},\quad\theta_{|t=0}=\theta^{0}.\end{array}\right.

Here, e2e_{2} denotes the vector (0,1),(0,1), v=(v1,v2)v=(v_{1},v_{2}) is the velocity field, π\pi the scalar pressure and θ\theta the temperature. The coefficients ν\nu and κ\kappa are assumed to be positive; ν\nu is called the kinematic viscosity and κ\kappa the molecular conductivity.
In the case of strictly positive coefficients ν\nu and κ\kappa both velocity and temperature have sufficiently smoothing effects leading to the global well-posedness results proven by numerous authors in various function spaces (see [4, 9, 15] and the references therein).
For ν>0\nu>0 and κ=0\kappa=0 the problem of global well-posedness is well understood. In [5], Chae proved global well-posedness for initial data (v0,θ0)(v^{0},\theta^{0}) lying in Sobolev spaces Hs×Hs,H^{s}\times H^{s}, with s>2s>2 ( see also [14]). This result has been recently improved in [11] by taking the data in Hs×Hs,H^{s}\times H^{s}, with s>0.s>0. However we give only a global existence result without uniqueness in the energy space L2×L2.L^{2}\times L^{2}. In [1] we prove a uniqueness result for data belonging to L2∩B∞,1−1×B2,10.L^{2}\cap B_{\infty,1}^{-1}\times B_{2,1}^{0}. More recently Danchin and Paicu [8] have established a uniqueness result in the energy space.

Our goal here is to study the global well-posedness of the system (B0,κ),(B_{0,\kappa}), with κ>0.\kappa>0. First of all, let us recall that the two-dimensional incompressible Euler system, corresponding to θ0=0,\theta^{0}=0, is globally well-posed in the Sobolev space Hs,H^{s}, with s>2.s>2. This is due to the advection of the vorticity by the flow: there is no accumulation of the vorticity and thus there is no finite time singularities according to B-K-M criterion [3]. In critical spaces like Bp,12p+1B_{p,1}^{\frac{2}{p}+1} the situation is more complicate because we do not know if the B-K-M criterion works or not. In [16], Vishik proved that Euler system is globally well-posed in these critical Besov spaces. He used for the proof a new logarithmic estimate taking advantage on the particular structure of the vorticity equation in dimension two. For the Boussinesq system (B0,κ)(B_{0,\kappa}), Chae has proved in [5] the global well-posedness for initial data v0,θ0v^{0},\theta^{0} lying in Soboloev space Hs,H^{s}, with s>2,s>2, His method is basically related to Sobolev logarithmic estimate in which the velocity and the temperature are needed to be Lipschitzian explaining the restriction s>2.s>2. We intend here to improve this result for rough initial data. Our results reads as follows (see the definition of Besov spaces given in next section ).

Theorem 1.1.

Let v0∈Bp,11+2pv^{0}\in B_{p,1}^{1+\frac{2}{p}} be a divergence-free vector field of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} and θ0∈Lr,\theta^{0}\in L^{r}, with 2<r≤p<∞2<r\leq p<\infty . Then there exists a unique global solution (v,θ)(v,\theta) to the Boussinesq system (B0,κ),κ>0(B_{0,\kappa}),\kappa>0 such that

v∈𝒞⁡(ℝ+,Bp,11+2p)andθ∈L∞​(ℝ+,Lr)∩L~loc1​(ℝ+,Br,∞2).v\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbb{R}_{+};B_{p,1}^{1+\frac{2}{p}})\,\quad\hbox{and}\quad\theta\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{r})\cap\widetilde{L}^{1}_{\textnormal{loc}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};B_{r,\infty}^{2}).

The situation in the case p=+∞p=+\infty is more subtle since Leray’s projector is not continuous on L∞L^{\infty} and we overcome this by working in homogeneous Besov spaces leading to more technical difficulties. Before stating our result we introduce the following sub-space of L∞:L^{\infty}:

u∈ℬ∞⇔‖u‖ℬ∞:=‖u‖L∞+‖Δ−1​u‖B˙∞,10<∞.u\in\mathcal{B}^{\infty}\Leftrightarrow\|u\|_{\mathcal{B}^{\infty}}:=\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\Delta_{-1}u\|_{\dot{B}_{\infty,1}^{0}}<\infty.

We notice that ℬ∞\mathcal{B}^{\infty} is a Banach space and independent of the choice of the unity dyadic partition. For the definition of the frequency localization operator Δ−1\Delta_{-1} we can see next section. Our second main result is the following:

Theorem 1.2.

Let v0∈B∞,11,v^{0}\in B_{\infty,1}^{1}, with zero divergence and θ0∈ℬ∞\theta^{0}\in\mathcal{B}^{\infty} . Then there exists a unique global solution (v,θ)(v,\theta) to the Boussinesq system (B0,κ),κ>0(B_{0,\kappa}),\kappa>0 such that

v∈𝒞⁡(ℝ+,B∞,11)andθ∈Lloc∞​(ℝ+,ℬ∞)∩L~loc1​(ℝ+,B∞,∞2).v\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbb{R}_{+};B_{\infty,1}^{1})\,\quad\hbox{and}\quad\theta\in L^{\infty}_{\textnormal{loc}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\mathcal{B}^{\infty})\cap\widetilde{L}^{1}_{\textnormal{loc}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};B_{\infty,\infty}^{2}).

The key of the proof is to bound for every time Lipschitz norm of both velocity and temperature. This will be done by using some logarithmic estimates and Theorem 3.1. The last one describes new smoothing effects for the transport-diffusion equation governed by a vector field which is not necessary Lipschitzian but only quasi-lipschitzian. Its proof is done in the spirit of [11].

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In section 22, we recall some preliminary results on Besov spaces. Section 33 is devoted to the proof of smoothing effects. In section 44 and 55 we give respectively the proof of Theorem 1.1 and 1.2. We give in the appendix a logarithmic estimate and a commutator lemma.

3. Smoothing effects

This section is devoted to the proof of a new regularization effect for a transport-diffusion equation with respect to a vector field which is not necessary Lipschitzian. This problem was studied by the first author [11] in the context of singular vortex patches for two dimensional Navier-Stokes equations. The estimate given below is more precise.

Theorem 3.1.

Let vv be a smooth divergence-free vector field of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with vorticity ω:=curl ​v.\omega:=\textnormal{curl }v. Let aa be a smooth solution of the transport-diffusion equation

∂ta+v⋅∇a−Δa=0;a|t=0=a0.\partial_{t}a+v\cdot\nabla a-\Delta a=0;\quad a_{|t=0}=a^{0}.

Then we have for q∈ℕ∪{−1}q\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{-1\} and t≥0t\geq 0

22​q​∫0t‖Δq​a​(τ)‖L∞​𝑑τ\displaystyle 2^{2q}\int_{0}^{t}\|\Delta_{q}a(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∥a0∥L∞(1+t+(q+2)∥ω∥Lt1​L∞+∥∇Δ−1v∥Lt1​L∞).\displaystyle\|a^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}\Big(1+t+(q+2)\|\omega\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}+\|\nabla\Delta_{-1}v\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}\Big).

We restrict ourselves to the a priori estimates. The existence and uniqueness parts are easily obtained with small modifications of the proof of Theorem 1.2.

5. Proof of Theorem 1.2

The case p=+∞p=+\infty is more subtle and the difficulty comes from the term ∥∇Δ−1v∥L∞,\|\nabla\Delta_{-1}v\|_{L^{\infty}}, since Riesz transforms do not map L∞L^{\infty} to itself. To avoid this problem we use a frequency interpolation method. The proof will be done in several steps. The first one deals with some a priori estimates. We give in the second the uniqueness result and the last is reserved to the proof of the existence part.

5.1. A priori estimates

The main result of this section is the following:

Proposition 5.1.

There exists a constant C0C_{0} depending on ‖v0‖B∞,10\|v^{0}\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}} and ‖θ0‖L∞\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}} such that for t∈[0,∞[t\in[0,\infty[

‖θ⁡(t)‖L∞≤‖θ0‖L∞;‖θ‖Lt1​B∞,11\displaystyle\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}};\quad\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,1}^{1}} ≤\displaystyle\leq C0​eC0​t3and\displaystyle C_{0}e^{C_{0}t^{3}}\quad\hbox{and}
‖v‖L~t∞​B∞,11+‖θ‖L~t1​B∞,∞2+‖θ⁡(t)‖ℬ∞\displaystyle\|v\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\infty}_{t}B_{\infty,1}^{1}}+\|\theta\|_{\widetilde{L}^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,\infty}^{2}}+\|\theta(t)\|_{\mathcal{B}^{\infty}} ≤\displaystyle\leq C0​eeC0​t3.\displaystyle C_{0}e^{e^{C_{0}t^{3}}}.
Proof.

The L∞L^{\infty}-bound of the temperature can be easily obtained from the maximum principle. To give the other bounds we start with the following estimate for the vorticity, which is again a direct consequence of the maximum principle,

(20) ‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞≤‖ω0‖L∞+‖∇θ‖Lt1​L∞≤‖ω0‖L∞+‖θ‖Lt1​B∞,11.\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|\omega^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\nabla\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}\leq\|\omega^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,1}^{1}}.

Lemma 5.2.

For all t≥0,t\geq 0, wed have

∥∇Δ−1v(t)∥L∞≲1+log(e+∥v0∥L∞+t∥θ0∥L∞)∥ω∥Lt∞​L∞+t∥ω∥Lt∞​L∞2.\|\nabla\Delta_{-1}v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim 1+\log\big(e+\|v^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+t\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}\big)\|\omega\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{\infty}}+t\|\omega\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{\infty}}^{2}.

+\displaystyle+ ∫0t‖S˙−M​div​𝒫​(v⊗v)​(τ)‖L∞​𝑑τ\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\|\dot{S}_{-M}\textnormal{div}\hskip 1.9919pt\mathcal{P}(v\otimes v)(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖v0‖L∞+t​‖θ0‖L∞+2−M​∫0t‖v⁡(τ)‖L∞2​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\|v^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+t\|\theta^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+2^{-M}\int_{0}^{t}\|v(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}d\tau.

5.3. Existence part

We will briefly outline the proof of the existence part which is classical. We smooth out the initial data (vn0,θn0):=(Sn​v0,Sn​θ0),(v_{n}^{0},\theta_{n}^{0}):=(S_{n}v^{0},S_{n}\theta^{0}), which is uniformly bounded in B∞,11×ℬ∞B_{\infty,1}^{1}\times\mathcal{B}^{\infty} and it is easy to check the following convergence result

limn→∞(‖vn0−v0‖B∞,10+∑q≤0‖Δ˙q​(θn0−θ0)‖L∞+‖θn0−θ0‖B∞,∞−12)=0.\lim_{n\to\infty}\Big(\|v_{n}^{0}-v^{0}\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}+\sum_{q\leq 0}\|\dot{\Delta}_{q}(\theta_{n}^{0}-\theta^{0})\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\theta^{0}_{n}-\theta^{0}\|_{B_{\infty,\infty}^{\frac{-1}{2}}}\Big)=0.

Since the initial data (vn0,θn0)(v_{n}^{0},\theta^{0}_{n}) are smooth then the corresponding Boussinesq system has global unique smooth solutions (vn,θn).(v_{n},\theta_{n}). In view of Proposition 5.1 one has for every t∈ℝ+,t\in\mathbb{R}_{+}, the uniform estimates:

‖vn‖Lt∞​B∞,11+‖θn​(t)‖L∞+‖∇θn‖Lt1​L∞≤C0​eeC0​t3.\|v_{n}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}B_{\infty,1}^{1}}+\|\theta_{n}(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\nabla\theta_{n}\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}\leq C_{0}e^{e^{C_{0}t^{3}}}.

Now according to (32) the sequence (vn,θn)n(v_{n},\theta_{n})_{n} converges strongly in Lloc∞​(ℝ+,B∞,10)×Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,B˙∞,10)L^{\infty}_{\textnormal{loc}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};B_{\infty,1}^{0})\times L^{1}_{\textnormal{l}oc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\dot{B}_{\infty,1}^{0}) to (v,θ).(v,\theta). This is sufficiently to pass to the limit in the equations and deduce that (v,θ)(v,\theta) satisfies the system (B0,κ).(B_{0,\kappa}).
It remains to show the continuity in time of the velocity. This comes from the estimate ‖v‖L~t∞​B∞,11,\|v\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\infty}_{t}B_{\infty,1}^{1}}, (see [12] for more further details).

The proof of Theorem 1.2 is now complete.

Appendix A. Logarithmic estimate

We shall now give a logarithmic estimate which is an extension of Vishik’s one [16]. Our result was firstly proved in [13] and for the convenience of the reader we will give here the proof.

Proposition 5.3.

Let p,r∈[1,+∞],p,\,r\in[1,+\infty], vv be a divergence-free vector field belonging to the space Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,Lip​(ℝd))L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\textnormal{Lip}(\mathbb{R}^{d})) and let aa be a smooth solution of the following equation ((with ν≥0\nu\geq 0)),

{∂ta+v⋅∇a−ν​Δ​a=fa|t=0=a0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}a+v\cdot\nabla a-\nu\Delta a=f\\ {a}_{|t=0}=a^{0}.\\ \end{array}\right.

If the initial data a0∈Bp,r0,a^{0}\in B_{p,r}^{0}, then we have for all t∈ℝ+t\in\mathbb{R}_{+}

‖a‖L~t∞​Bp,r0≤C⁡(‖a0‖Bp,r0+‖f‖L~t1​Bp,r0)​(1+∫0t‖∇v​(τ)‖L∞​𝑑τ),\|a\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\infty}_{t}B_{p,r}^{0}}\leq C\big(\|a^{0}\|_{B_{p,r}^{0}}+\|f\|_{\widetilde{L}^{1}_{t}B_{p,r}^{0}}\big)\Big(1+\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau\Big),

where CC depends only on the dimension dd but not on the viscosity ν.\nu.

Proof.

We denote by a~q\tilde{a}_{q} the unique global solution of the initial value problem:

{∂ta~q+v⋅∇a~q−Δ​a~q=Δq​f:=fqa~q​(0)=Δq​a0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\tilde{a}_{q}+v\cdot\nabla\tilde{a}_{q}-\Delta\tilde{a}_{q}=\Delta_{q}f:=f_{q}\\ {\tilde{a}_{q}}{(0)}=\Delta_{q}a^{0}.\\ \end{array}\right.

Using Proposition 2.3 with r=+∞r=+\infty and s=±12,s=\pm\frac{1}{2}, one obtains

‖a~q​(t)‖Bp,∞±12≲(‖Δq​a0‖Bp,∞±12+∫0t‖fq​(τ)‖Bp,∞±12​𝑑τ)​eC​∫0t‖∇v​(τ)‖L∞​𝑑τ.\|\tilde{a}_{q}(t)\|_{B_{p,\infty}^{\pm\frac{1}{2}}}\lesssim\Big(\|\Delta_{q}{a}^{0}\|_{B_{p,\infty}^{\pm\frac{1}{2}}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|f_{q}(\tau)\|_{B_{p,\infty}^{\pm\frac{1}{2}}}d\tau\Big)e^{C\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_{{L^{\infty}}}d\tau}.

Thus we deduce from the definition of Besov spaces that for all j≥−1j\geq-1

(33) ‖Δj​a~q‖Lt∞​Lp≲2−12​|q−j|​(‖Δq​a0‖Lp+‖fq‖Lt1​Lp)​eV⁡(t),\|\Delta_{j}\tilde{a}_{q}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}}\lesssim 2^{-\frac{1}{2}|q-j|}\Big(\|\Delta_{q}{a}^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\|f_{q}\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{p}}\Big)e^{V(t)},

with V⁡(t):=C​∫0t‖∇v​(τ)‖L∞​𝑑τ.V(t):={C\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau}. Now by linearity one can write

a⁡(t,x)=∑q≥−1a~q​(t,x).a(t,x)=\sum_{q\geq-1}\tilde{a}_{q}(t,x).

Taking N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} that will be carefully chosen later. Then we write by definition

(34) ‖a‖L~t∞​Bp,r0\displaystyle\|a\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\infty}_{t}B_{p,r}^{0}} ≤\displaystyle\leq (∑j(∑q‖Δj​a~q‖Lt∞​Lp)r)1r\displaystyle\Big(\sum_{j}\Big(\sum_{q}\|\Delta_{j}\tilde{a}_{q}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}}\Big)^{r}\Big)^{\frac{1}{r}}
≤\displaystyle\leq (∑j(∑|q−j|≥N‖Δj​a~q‖Lt∞​Lp)r)1r+(∑j(∑|q−j|<N‖Δj​a~q‖Lt∞​Lp)r)1r\displaystyle\Big(\sum_{j}\Big(\sum_{|q-j|\geq N}\|\Delta_{j}\tilde{a}_{q}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}}\Big)^{r}\Big)^{\frac{1}{r}}+\Big(\sum_{j}\Big(\sum_{|q-j|<N}\|\Delta_{j}\tilde{a}_{q}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}}\Big)^{r}\Big)^{\frac{1}{r}}
=\displaystyle= I+II.\displaystyle\hbox{I}+\hbox{II}.

To estimate the first term we use (33) and the convolution inequality

(35) I ≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2−12​N​eV⁡(t)​‖(‖aq0‖Lp+‖fq‖Lt1​Lp)q‖ℓr\displaystyle 2^{-\frac{1}{2}N}e^{V(t)}\|\big(\|{a_{q}}^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\|f_{q}\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{p}}\big)_{q}\|_{\ell^{r}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2−12​N​eV⁡(t)​(‖a0‖Bp,r0+‖f‖L~t1​Bp,r0).\displaystyle 2^{-\frac{1}{2}N}e^{V(t)}\Big(\|a^{0}\|_{B_{p,r}^{0}}+\|f\|_{\widetilde{L}^{1}_{t}B_{p,r}^{0}}\Big).

To treat the second term of the right-hand side of (34), we use two facts: the first one is that the operator Δj\Delta_{j} maps uniformly LpL^{p} into itself while the second is the LpL^{p} energy estimate. So we find

(36) II ≲\displaystyle\lesssim (∑j(∑|q−j|<N‖a~q‖Lt∞​Lp)r)1r\displaystyle\Big(\sum_{j}\Big(\sum_{|q-j|<N}\|\tilde{a}_{q}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}}\Big)^{r}\Big)^{\frac{1}{r}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim (∑j(∑|q−j|<N‖aq0‖Lp+‖fq‖Lt1​Lp)r)1r\displaystyle\Big(\sum_{j}\Big(\sum_{|q-j|<N}\|{a}_{q}^{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\|f_{q}\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{p}}\Big)^{r}\Big)^{\frac{1}{r}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim N⁡(‖a0‖Bp,r0+‖f‖L~t1​Bp,r0).\displaystyle N\big(\|a^{0}\|_{B_{p,r}^{0}}+\|f\|_{\widetilde{L}^{1}_{t}B_{p,r}^{0}}\big).

Plugging estimates (35) and () into (34), we have

‖a‖L~t∞​Bp,r0≲(‖a0‖Bp,r0+‖f‖L~t1​Bp,r0)​(2−12​N​eV⁡(t)+N).\|a\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\infty}_{t}B_{p,r}^{0}}\lesssim\big(\|a^{0}\|_{B_{p,r}^{0}}+\|f\|_{\widetilde{L}^{1}_{t}B_{p,r}^{0}}\big)\big(2^{-\frac{1}{2}N}e^{V(t)}+N\big).

Taking

N=[2​V​(t)log⁡2+1],N=\Big[\frac{2V(t)}{\log 2}+1\Big],

leads to the desired inequality. ∎

Appendix B. Commutator estimate

Our task now is to prove the following commutator result.

Proposition 5.4.

Let uu be a smooth function and vv be a divergence-free vector field of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} such that its vorticity ω:=curl ​v\omega:=\hbox{curl }v belongs to L∞.L^{\infty}. Then we have for all q≥−1,q\geq-1,

∥[Δq,v⋅∇]u∥L∞≲∥u∥L∞(∥∇Δ−1v∥L∞+(q+2)∥ω∥L∞).\big\|[\Delta_{q},v\cdot\nabla]u\big\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}\Big(\|\nabla\Delta_{-1}v\|_{L^{\infty}}+(q+2)\|\omega\|_{L^{\infty}}\Big).
Proof.

The principal tool is Bony’s decomposition [2]:

(37) [Δq,v⋅∇]u=[Δq,Tv⋅∇]u+[Δq,T∇⁣⋅⋅v]u+[Δq,R(v⋅∇,.)]u,[\Delta_{q},v\cdot\nabla]u=[\Delta_{q},T_{v}\cdot\nabla]u+[\Delta_{q},T_{\nabla\cdot}\cdot v]u+[\Delta_{q},R(v\cdot\nabla,.)]u,

where

[Δq,Tv⋅∇]u=Δq(Tv⋅∇u)−Tv⋅∇Δqu\displaystyle[\Delta_{q},T_{v}\cdot\nabla]u=\Delta_{q}(T_{v}\cdot\nabla u)-T_{v}\cdot\nabla\Delta_{q}u
[Δq,T∇⁣⋅⋅v]u=Δq(T∇u⋅v)−T∇Δqu⋅v\displaystyle[\Delta_{q},T_{\nabla\cdot}\cdot v]u=\Delta_{q}(T_{\nabla u}\cdot v)-T_{\nabla\Delta_{q}u}\cdot v
[Δq,R(v⋅∇,.)]u=Δq(R(v⋅∇,u))−R(v⋅∇,Δqu).\displaystyle[\Delta_{q},R(v\cdot\nabla,.)]u=\Delta_{q}(R(v\cdot\nabla,u))-R(v\cdot\nabla,\Delta_{q}u).

From the definition of the paraproduct and according to Bernstein inequalities

(38) ‖[Δq,T∇⁣⋅⋅v]​u‖L∞\displaystyle\|[\Delta_{q},T_{\nabla\cdot}\cdot v]u\|_{L^{\infty}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑|j−q|≤4∥Sj−1∇u∥L∞∥Δjv∥L∞\displaystyle\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}\|S_{j-1}\nabla u\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\Delta_{j}v\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖u‖L∞​‖ω‖L∞,\displaystyle\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\omega\|_{L^{\infty}},

where we have used here the following equivalence: ∀j∈ℕ,\forall j\in\mathbb{N},

‖Δj​v‖L∞≈2−j​‖Δj​ω‖L∞.\|\Delta_{j}v\|_{L^{\infty}}\approx 2^{-j}\|\Delta_{j}\omega\|_{L^{\infty}}.

For the second term of the right-hand side of (37), we have

[Δq,Tv⋅∇]u\displaystyle[\Delta_{q},T_{v}\cdot\nabla]u =\displaystyle= ∑j≥1[Δq,Sj−1​v⋅∇Δj]​u,\displaystyle\sum_{j\geq 1}[\Delta_{q},S_{j-1}v\cdot\nabla\Delta_{j}]u,
=\displaystyle= ∑|j−q|≤4[Δq,Sj−1v⋅∇]Δju.\displaystyle\sum_{|j-q|\leq 4}[\Delta_{q},S_{j-1}v\cdot\nabla]\Delta_{j}u.

To estimate each commutator, we write Δq\Delta_{q} as a convolution

[Δq,Sj−1v⋅∇]Δju(x)=2q​d∫h(2q(x−y))(Sj−1v(y)−Sj−1v(x))⋅∇Δju(y)dy.\displaystyle[\Delta_{q},S_{j-1}v\cdot\nabla]\Delta_{j}u(x)=2^{qd}\int h(2^{q}(x-y))\big(S_{j-1}v(y)-S_{j-1}v(x)\big)\cdot\nabla\Delta_{j}u(y)dy.

Thus, Young and Bernstein inequalities yield, for |j−q|≤4,|j-q|\leq 4,

(39) ∥[Δq,Sj−1v⋅∇]Δju∥L∞\displaystyle\qquad\big\|[\Delta_{q},S_{j-1}v\cdot\nabla]\Delta_{j}u\big\|_{L^{\infty}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2−q∥∇Sj−1v∥L∞∥Δj∇u∥L∞\displaystyle 2^{-q}\|\nabla S_{j-1}v\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\Delta_{j}\nabla u\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∥∇Sj−1v∥L∞∥u∥L∞\displaystyle\|\nabla S_{j-1}v\|_{L^{\infty}}\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim (∥∇Δ−1v∥L∞+(q+2)∥ω∥L∞)∥u∥L∞.\displaystyle\Big(\|\nabla\Delta_{-1}v\|_{L^{\infty}}+(q+2)\|\omega\|_{L^{\infty}}\Big)\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}.

Let us move to the remainder term. It can be written, in view of the definition, as

Jq:=[Δq,R(v⋅∇,.)]u=∑j≥q−4,j≥0i∈{∓1,0}[Δq,Δjv]⋅∇Δj+iu+∑i∈{0,1}[Δq,Δ−1v]⋅∇Δ−1+iu.\hbox{J}_{q}:=[\Delta_{q},{R}(v\cdot\nabla,.)]u=\sum_{j\geq q-4,j\geq 0\atop\\ i\in\{\mp 1,0\}}[\Delta_{q},\Delta_{j}v]\cdot\nabla\Delta_{j+i}u+\sum_{i\in\{0,1\}}[\Delta_{q},\Delta_{-1}v]\cdot\nabla\Delta_{-1+i}u.

It follows from the zero divergence condition that

Jq=∑i∈{0,1}[Δq,Δ−1v]⋅∇Δ−1+iu+∑j≥q−4,j≥0i∈{∓1,0}div ([Δq,Δjv]⊗Δj+iu)=Jq1+Jq2.\hbox{J}_{q}=\sum_{i\in\{0,1\}}[\Delta_{q},\Delta_{-1}v]\cdot\nabla\Delta_{-1+i}u+\sum_{j\geq q-4,j\geq 0\atop\\ i\in\{\mp 1,0\}}\textnormal{div }\big([\Delta_{q},\Delta_{j}v]\otimes\Delta_{j+i}u\big)\\ =\hbox{J}_{q}^{1}+\hbox{J}_{q}^{2}.

By the same way as (39) one has

‖Jq1‖L2\displaystyle\|\hbox{J}_{q}^{1}\|_{L^{2}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2−q∥∇Δ−1v∥L∞∑i=01∥∇Δ−1+iu∥L∞\displaystyle 2^{-q}\|\nabla\Delta_{-1}v\|_{L^{\infty}}\sum_{i=0}^{1}\|\nabla\Delta_{-1+i}u\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∥∇Δ−1v∥L∞∥u∥L∞.\displaystyle\|\nabla\Delta_{-1}v\|_{L^{\infty}}\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}.

To estimate the second term we use Bernstein inequality

‖Jq2‖L2\displaystyle\|\hbox{J}_{q}^{2}\|_{L^{2}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∑j≥q−4,j≥0i∈{∓1,0}2q​‖Δj​v‖L∞​‖Δj+i​u‖L∞\displaystyle\sum_{j\geq q-4,j\geq 0\atop i\in\{\mp 1,0\}}2^{q}\|\Delta_{j}v\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\Delta_{j+i}u\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖u‖L∞​∑j≥q−42q−j​‖Δj​ω‖L∞\displaystyle\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}\sum_{j\geq q-4}2^{q-j}\|\Delta_{j}\omega\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖ω‖L∞​‖u‖L∞,\displaystyle\|\omega\|_{L^{\infty}}\|u\|_{L^{\infty}},

This completes the proof of Proposition 5.4. ∎
